Stop us if you’ve heard this one before… 🛑

But if want your baby to eat the types of foods that you eat, without the need for making separate meals: 

Serve them food the way you like to eat it. 

With: 

✔️ Color 
✔️ Texture 
✔️ Flavor 
✔️ Variety 

The reason so many toddlers prefer bland foods is because many parents assume that’s all they can have when they start solids (think: rice cereal & oatmeal), so of course babies develop a preference for bland foods. 

But you can actually begin introducing flavor, texture, and different ingredients (even spice!) as soon as your baby is ready to start solids. This is typically around 6 months. 

⚠️ Remember: Egg is one of THE most common food allergens and should be introduced separately from other foods so you can rule out potential allergies. This video shows pesto (which often contains nuts) as well as Parmesan cheese. Before offering or mixing allergens, be sure you’ve introduced the common ones separately from other foods first. 

If this feels scary to you, our app walks you through daily allergen introduction on a safe schedule. We even show you how to use it in recipes so you can keep that oh-so-important allergen exposure up!

Your baby doesn’t need teeth to eat real food! 🍍

Wondering what foods your 6-month-old baby can eat? You might be surprised by how many options you have. 

From steak and chicken to pasta, broccoli, and pineapple, babies can explore a wide variety of flavours and textures from around 6 months old. 

The key isn’t how many teeth your baby has — it’s whether they’re showing signs of readiness for starting solids and whether food is prepared safely for their age and developmental stage.

5 foods your baby can explore from 6 months:

🥩 Steak
🍝 Pasta
🍗 Chicken
🥦 Broccoli
🍍 Pineapple

Remember: Every baby develops at their own pace. Always check for readiness signs, offer appropriately prepared foods, and supervise your baby while eating.

🔎 Search hundreds of foods in the Solid Starts app

📲 SHARE with a parent who’s getting ready to start solids!

Follow @solidstarts for more baby-led weaning tips, first foods inspiration, and practical advice for introducing solids with confidence. 🤍

Starting solids doesn’t mean your baby is suddenly going to start eating full meals overnight 🥩🥦🥔🍝

Social media can make it seem like every baby is sitting down and eating huge plates of food from day one, but the reality is that this isn’t typical for most babies. 🤍

Some babies take to solids quickly, while others need more time to explore, touch, squish, taste, and get comfortable with new foods. And that’s completely normal. 

In the beginning, it’s not about how much food your baby actually eats. Prior to 12 months, breastmilk and/or formula should be your baby’s primary source of nutrition. Introducing solid food is all about helping them explore, learn, and build exposure to new foods and  allergens. Success looks different for everyone, but the goal is building familiarity, developing skills, and creating positive experiences around food.

✨ If your baby is showing interest, exploring different foods, and gradually becoming more comfortable at mealtimes, you’re on the right track!

Try not to compare your baby’s plate to what you see on Instagram. Every baby learns at their own pace, and progress doesn’t always look like an empty plate. 🤍

Wait wait - don’t scroll 😂

Yes, that’s chicken liver, but stay with us… 

Chicken liver is SO nutritious for babies when starting solids but often overlooked. It’s rich in fat and protein, in addition to choline, iron, folate, selenium, zinc, and vitamins A, B12, and other B vitamins. Together, these nutrients support baby’s energy to play and explore, brain development, growth, strength, red blood cells, hormones, immune function, taste perception, vision, and metabolic processes! 

Whew! 😅

Additionally, introducing your baby to a wide variety of foods and flavors, even ones you may not love yourself, helps them to accept a variety of foods later on! 

⚠️ Note: Chicken liver has high levels of vitamin A. Vitamin A is an essential nutrient, but can be toxic when consumed in excess. For this reason, take care to limit the serving size and frequency; 1 to 2 tablespoons of chicken liver once a week is plenty.

Solid Starts

Wean with it, rock with it. May the odds be ever in your flavor…😉🪨📄✂️

But here’s the thing: when it comes to starting solids, it’s not about winning or losing. 

Purées, finger foods, or a little bit of both? There’s room for all of it!

Every baby learns at their own pace, every family finds their own rhythm, and no two feeding journeys look exactly alike.

🥄 Okay, so what’s wrong with spoonfeeding? Around here we talk about the many benefits of baby-led weaning, which means: letting baby lead. The research tells us that the risk of choking is minimized when a baby brings food to their own mouth and that placing food into their mouth increases risk. Spoonfeeding, while perfectly acceptable as a method for feeding baby, does not allow baby to self-feed. And our goal here is to offer the safest approach backed by research. 

🥣 But why no purees? To be clear, we love purées! There’s nothing wrong with offering purées, but offer them in combination with chewable foods to give baby the safest start. Learning to chew is important between 6-9 mos and babies can’t do that with only textureless food. 

The real win here is helping your little one explore new foods, build confidence, and enjoy the adventure (mess and all). The goal is let baby lead the way.🤍

Strawberries can help your baby absorb MORE iron 👀

Strawberries aren’t particularly high in iron themselves, but they’re rich in vitamin C, which helps your baby’s body absorb non-heme iron (the type found in plant-based foods).

And that’s especially important when starting solids. 

Around 6 months, babies’ iron stores begin to decline, making iron-rich foods an important part of their diet.

Try pairing strawberries with:

🥣 Iron-fortified baby oatmeal
🫘 Lentils or beans
🌱 Tofu
🥜 Smooth, thinned nut butter (once you’ve ruled out allergies)

Want to know how to safely serve each of these foods?
